Agatha Christie. A British mystery writer and the bestselling novelist of all time, credited with writing sixty-six detective novels and numerous short stories. Born in Devon to an upper-middle-class family, she was married and widowed, and turned to writing mystery novels during her first marriage to support herself. Her ingenious plots, fair-play mysteries, and iconic detectives defined the golden age of detective fiction. Her most famous creation was Hercule Poirot, a fastidious Belgian detective with a little grey cells, who appeared in thirty-nine novels and numerous short stories over six decades. She also created Miss Marple, an elderly spinster living in a quiet English village who solves crimes through her knowledge of human nature. Miss Marple appeared in twelve novels spanning Christie's career. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, published in nineteen twenty-six, was a landmark mystery where the detective Poirot investigates a wealthy man's death, and it became famous for its narrative twist. Murder on the Orient Express, from nineteen thirty-four, features Poirot investigating a murder aboard a luxury train snowbound in the Alps; it exemplifies elegant and intricate plotting. And Then There Were None, published in nineteen thirty-nine, remains her masterpiece: ten strangers invited to an island are killed one by one according to a nursery rhyme. It is considered one of the greatest mystery novels ever written. Christie also wrote The Mousetrap, a stage play about strangers snowed in at a guest house where a murderer strikes. Premiered in nineteen fifty-two, it ran for over seventy years, becoming the longest-running play in theatrical history. Through her work, Christie became the most-performed playwright in the world.
